newsitem.title: USA: US slowing seems to have persisted - Fed's Broaddus.
newsitem.headline: US slowing seems to have persisted - Fed's Broaddus.

text.p: Alfred Broaddus, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond, said Wednesday a slowing in the economy that began in the summer appears to have persisted, a development he welcomed.

Speaking to the American Furniture Manufacturers Association, Broaddus said gross domestic product growth slowed sharply in the third quarter, to an annual rate of 2.0 percent from 4.7 percent in the second quarter.
"It does appear that this deceleration has persisted in the current quarter," he said.
Broaddus said the slowing scenario was consistent with recent employment data.

Figures from the Labor Department show U.S. nonfarm payrolls grew by a moderate 118,000 in November following a 224,000 gain in October. The unemployment rate edged up to 5.4 percent from 5.2 percent.
The Richmond Fed chief said the cooling down of growth was a healthy sign.

"My own feeling is that this is definitely a good thing because it tends to support the current prediction of a majority of national economic forecasters that the economy is now decelerating to a growth rate that is more sustainable over the longer term," Broaddus said.
He added, "A little less growth now probably will reduce the risk of a boom developing situation as we go forward, which would darken the outlook."
Turning to inflation, the Fed official said recent figures had been good. "The recent inflation reports have been very encouraging," he said.
The Labor Department's Consumer Price Index has been rising at an annual rate of 3.0 percent. The November CPI report is due Thursday at 0830 EST/1330 GMT.
Looking at the longer-term strategy on inflation, Broaddus said the Fed must reduce it further.
He said a policy of accepting a 3.0 percent annual CPI rise would not be perceived as credible.

"We need to try to move, over the long haul, the CPI inflation rate down toward 2.0 percent and ultimately below 2.0 percent, and then hold it there and convince everyone that this is the center of gravity," he said.
Broaddus was asked about a recent report concluding that the CPI was overstated by 1.1 percentage points a year.

He said the idea that the CPI was overstated was not new and that the Fed would be reviewing the report in detail. "We at the Fed need to look at that report carefully and see what kinds of ways may be available to improve our policy action," he said.
The CPI report was prepared by a congressionally appointed commission led by Stanford Unversity economist Michael Boskin.
